subtitle: How a Bombay merchant weighed an empire and found it wanting

panels.shot: dramatic three-quarter view, low-angle, with ledgers and maps of India and Britain behind him like looming shadows
panels.action: Dadabhai Naoroji stands at a heavy wooden desk, one hand on a ledger, the other on a map of India and Britain, his face calm yet unyielding as stormy clouds gather beyond a window.

dialogue.text: In an age of empire and famine, Dadabhai Naoroji turned to numbers, and quietly declared that British rule itself was draining India dry.

i18n.hi: साम्राज्य और अकाल के दौर में दादाभाई नौरोजी ने आँकड़ों का सहारा लिया, और चुपचाप कहा – खुद अंग्रेजी राज ही भारत को सूखा रहा है।

panels.shot: slow push-in on Naoroji seated by a window, Bombay street beyond, quill poised over paper
panels.action: A younger Dadabhai Naoroji sits in a modest Bombay study, Parsi turban neatly tied, as bullock carts and barefoot labourers pass outside the open window.

dialogue.text: Bombay, 1860s. The new mills smoke, the docks bustle, yet in the lanes outside Dadabhai Naoroji’s window, hunger walks barefoot.

i18n.hi: बंबई, 1860 का दशक। नई मिलों से धुआँ, बंदरगाहों पर रौनक, पर नौरोजी की खिड़की के बाहर की गलियों में भूख नंगे पाँव चलती है।

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder close-up of Naoroji’s hand writing, faint reflection of his face in the inkpot
panels.action: Naoroji bends over his desk, writing in a neat hand as columns of figures, rupees and pounds, line his paper beside a small stack of government reports.

dialogue.text: Reports praise progress. Revenue rises, railways shine. Yet Naoroji sees something else in the figures: a river of wealth flowing outward, not back.

i18n.hi: रिपोर्टें तरक्की के गीत गाती हैं। आमदनी बढ़ती, रेलगाड़ियाँ चमकतीं। पर नौरोजी अंकों में कुछ और देखते हैं – दौलत की एक धारा जो बाहर बह रही है, लौटती नहीं।

panels.shot: split composition showing Indian peasants on one side and a London street with carriages on the other, both linked by a translucent stream of coins
panels.action: On one side, gaunt cultivators stand in a cracked field; on the other, a distant London boulevard glitters, the two scenes joined by an imagined stream of coins arcing from India to Britain.

dialogue.text: He starts to name the stream: high European salaries charged to India, pensions paid in London, military costs, profits remitted overseas without return.

i18n.hi: वह उस धारा के नाम गिनते हैं: ऊँची यूरोपीय तनख्वाहें भारत के खाते में, पेंशनें लंदन में, फौजी खर्च, और मुनाफे जो समुंदर पार चले जाते हैं, लौटकर नहीं आते।

panels.shot: medium shot, Naoroji addressing a small Bombay gathering in a hall lit by oil lamps
panels.action: Naoroji stands at a simple lectern in a Bombay hall, oil lamps casting shadows as a mixed crowd of merchants, clerks and students listens intently.

dialogue.speaker: dadabhai_naoroji
dialogue.text: We are told we are prospering. But look at our villages. Where is this wealth?

i18n.hi: कहते हैं हम अमीर हो रहे हैं। पर गाँवों को देखो। ये दौलत आखिर है कहाँ?

panels.shot: wide shot of a steamship at sea, low horizon, Naoroji standing at the rail looking toward the west
panels.action: On the deck of a smoke-belching steamship, Naoroji grips the rail, wind tugging at his coat as he watches the sun sink over the Arabian Sea towards Britain.

dialogue.text: To prove his suspicion, he decides, he must go to the heart of the empire itself, where budgets are drafted and India is spoken of as a ledger entry.

i18n.hi: शक साबित करने को वह ठानते हैं – उन्हें जाना होगा साम्राज्य के दिल में, वहाँ जहाँ बजट बनते हैं और ‘भारत’ बस एक खाते की लाइन बन कर रह जाता है।

panels.shot: establishing shot of Victorian London street in drizzle, Naoroji a small figure crossing with umbrella
panels.action: Under a grey London sky, Naoroji strides across a busy street, umbrella in hand, hansom cabs rushing past, stone buildings looming over this solitary Indian figure.

dialogue.text: London, late 1860s. The city hums with factories and finance. Here, the Indian merchant-teacher becomes something new: an economic critic of empire.

i18n.hi: लंदन, 1860 के आख़िरी साल। शहर कारखानों और बैंकों की गूँज से भरा। यहीं यह भारतीय व्यापारी-शिक्षक एक नई भूमिका पकड़ता है – साम्राज्य का आर्थिक आलोचक।

panels.shot: tight overhead shot of Naoroji’s desk piled with Blue Books, parliamentary papers and his own notes
panels.action: In a cramped London lodging, Naoroji sits amid stacks of British Blue Books and parliamentary papers, carefully copying tables into his own worn notebook.

dialogue.text: He mines official British statistics: revenues, exchange rates, military expenditure. With patient care, he begins to count what others have ignored.

i18n.hi: वह सरकारी ब्रिटिश आँकड़ों में गोता लगाते हैं – राजस्व, विनिमय दरें, फौजी खर्च। धैर्य से, वह उन चीज़ों की गिनती शुरू करते हैं जिन्हें सबने अनदेखा किया था।

panels.shot: close-up on Naoroji’s intense eyes as he reviews a page titled “Drain” in his notes
panels.action: Naoroji’s eyes narrow as he scans a page in his own hand where the word ‘Drain’ is underlined beside a rough estimate of India’s annual loss.

dialogue.text: In 1867 he lays out his idea: the ‘drain of wealth’ from India to Britain, perhaps tens of millions of rupees each year, taken without equivalent return.

i18n.hi: 1867 में वह अपना विचार साफ रखते हैं – भारत से ब्रिटेन की ओर ‘दौलत का निचोड़’, हर साल शायद करोड़ों रुपये, जिनका कोई बराबर बदला नहीं।

panels.shot: medium wide shot of Naoroji addressing a British audience in a lecture hall, some skeptical faces visible
panels.action: Naoroji stands on a London platform before a seated British audience, some leaning forward, others folding their arms, as he gestures towards a chart propped on an easel.

dialogue.speaker: dadabhai_naoroji
dialogue.text: If you call this rule ‘civilized’, then your justice must be just in fact, not in name.

i18n.hi: अगर आप इस राज को ‘सभ्य’ कहते हैं, तो आपकी इन्साफ़ सच में इन्साफ़ हो, सिर्फ़ नाम भर नहीं।

panels.shot: intimate medium shot, Naoroji in a London study drafting early versions of his arguments
panels.action: Late at night, Naoroji sits alone by a coal fire, writing the first outlines of what will become his book, the lamplight catching the tired lines on his face.

dialogue.text: He refines his case: foreign rule raises taxes, pushes peasants into debt, sends salaries and savings abroad. Poverty, he argues, is not a mystery. It is a system.

i18n.hi: वह अपनी दलील पैनी करते हैं – पराया राज टैक्स बढ़ाता है, किसान को कर्ज़ में डुबोता है, तनख्वाह और बचत विदेश भेजता है। गरीबी, वे कहते हैं, कोई पहेली नहीं – ये तो पूरी व्यवस्था है।

panels.shot: wide shot of an early Indian National Congress session, with Naoroji at the dais
panels.action: Back in India, Naoroji stands at the dais of an Indian National Congress session, rows of delegates in turbans and coats filling the hall, some taking notes, some nodding.

dialogue.text: Through the 1880s and 1890s, his figures travel home. In Congress presidential addresses, he links the drain to the demand for greater Indian control over revenues and administration.

i18n.hi: 1880–1890 के दशक में उनके आँकड़े वतन लौटते हैं। कांग्रेस के अध्यक्षीय भाषणों में वह ‘ड्रेन’ को जोड़ते हैं उस मांग से कि राजस्व और निज़ाम पर भारतीयों का बड़ा हक़ हो।

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Naoroji speaking from the Congress podium, hand raised slightly for emphasis
panels.action: Naoroji leans forward at the podium, one hand raised as the hall falls silent, delegates watching him with a mix of respect and urgency.

dialogue.speaker: dadabhai_naoroji
dialogue.text: We must have a share in the making of the budget. Without it, poverty will deepen.

i18n.hi: हमें बजट बनाने में हिस्सा चाहिए। इसके बिना गरीबी और गहरी होगी।

panels.shot: parliamentary gallery wide shot, Naoroji speaking at the green benches of the House of Commons
panels.action: Inside the House of Commons, Naoroji rises from a green bench, small among the rows of British MPs, yet steady as he holds out a sheaf of notes.

dialogue.text: In 1892, he goes further. Elected as a Liberal MP from Finsbury Central, he carries his drain tables into the British Parliament itself.

i18n.hi: 1892 में वह और आगे बढ़ते हैं। फिन्सबरी सेंट्रल से लिबरल एमपी चुनकर, वह अपने ‘ड्रेन’ वाले हिसाब सीधे ब्रिटिश संसद में ले जाते हैं।

panels.shot: medium close-up of Naoroji addressing Parliament, some MPs listening, others whispering
panels.action: Naoroji speaks earnestly in Parliament, a few MPs listening intently while others whisper to each other, the chamber’s carved wood and high ceiling looming above.

dialogue.speaker: dadabhai_naoroji
dialogue.text: You cannot draw the life-blood of a people and then wonder at their weakness.

i18n.hi: आप किसी कौम का ख़ून चूस कर फिर उसकी कमज़ोरी पर हैरान नहीं हो सकते।

panels.shot: tabletop shot of a printer’s workshop, stacks of freshly bound books titled on their spines
panels.action: In a quiet printing house, a worker stacks fresh copies of Naoroji’s book, their spines neat, while Naoroji examines one with care.

dialogue.text: By 1901, he gathers decades of speeches, calculations and correspondence into one work: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.

i18n.hi: 1901 तक वह दशकों के भाषण, हिसाब और चिट्ठियाँ एक किताब में समेटते हैं – ‘पॉवर्टी एंड अन-ब्रिटिश रूल इन इंडिया’।

panels.shot: close-up of the open book in Naoroji’s hands, his finger resting on a passage about ‘un-British rule’
panels.action: Naoroji holds the open book, finger resting on a section where he calls certain practices ‘un-British’, his expression calm but firm.

dialogue.text: He uses Britain’s own ideals as a measure. If rule creates chronic poverty and drains wealth, he argues, it is not just un-Indian. It is un-British by Britain’s claimed standards.

i18n.hi: वह खुद ब्रिटेन के आदर्शों को कसौटी बनाते हैं। अगर राज हमेशा की गरीबी बनाता है और दौलत निचोड़ता है, तो वह सिर्फ़ ग़ैर-भारतीय ही नहीं, ब्रिटेन के अपने दावे के हिसाब से ग़ैर-ब्रिटिश भी है।

panels.shot: wide shot of the 1906 Calcutta Congress session, Naoroji on stage addressing a large crowd
panels.action: At the 1906 Calcutta Congress, an elderly Naoroji stands supported by a lectern, before a sea of delegates under a vast pandal, punkahs swaying above.

dialogue.text: By 1906, the mood has shifted. Younger leaders press for a clearer goal. In his third presidential address, Naoroji gives their demand a word to rally around.

i18n.hi: 1906 तक हवा बदल चुकी है। नौजवान नेता साफ़ मंज़िल चाहते हैं। तीसरे अध्यक्षीय भाषण में नौरोजी उनकी मांग को एक नारा दे देते हैं।

panels.shot: medium close-up on Naoroji’s lined face as he speaks the word ‘Swaraj’
panels.action: Sweat beading on his brow, Naoroji looks out over the crowd, lips parted as he speaks, with a faint, determined smile.

dialogue.speaker: dadabhai_naoroji
dialogue.text: Self-government—Swaraj—is the only remedy for this drain and this poverty.

i18n.hi: स्वराज—ख़ुद अपना राज—ही इस ‘ड्रेन’ और गरीबी की एकमात्र दवा है।

panels.shot: montage-style wide shot: Indian students reading his book, British officials debating, village meeting under a banyan tree
panels.action: A montage shows an Indian student in London bent over Naoroji’s book, British officials in a committee room arguing over a report, and villagers under a banyan tree listening to a local leader explain new ideas about economic injustice.

dialogue.text: His estimates are debated, his arithmetic challenged. Yet the frame he offers—a rule that drains—spreads from lecture halls to village meetings, shaping how a generation thinks about empire.

i18n.hi: उनके अंदाज़ों पर बहस होती है, उनके हिसाब पर सवाल उठते हैं। फिर भी जो फ्रेम वह देते हैं – ऐसा राज जो निचोड़ता है – वह कॉलेजों से गाँव की चौपालों तक फैल जाता है, और एक पीढ़ी की नज़र में साम्राज्य का मतलब बदल देता है।

panels.shot: quiet close-up of an elderly Naoroji at his desk in later years, hand resting on old papers
panels.action: In his later years, an elderly Naoroji sits at a familiar desk, hand resting gently on a bundle of worn papers, as evening light filters through the window.

dialogue.text: Long before independence, Dadabhai Naoroji showed that the battle for freedom could begin with a ledger and a question: when the sums of power are written plainly, who can pretend not to see?

i18n.hi: आज़ादी से बहुत पहले, दादाभाई नौरोजी ने दिखा दिया कि लड़ाई एक खाता-बही और एक सवाल से भी शुरू हो सकती है – जब ताक़त के हिसाब साफ़-साफ़ लिखे जाएँ, तब कौन कह सकता है कि उसे दिखता ही नहीं?

subtitle_i18n.en: How a Bombay merchant weighed an empire and found it wanting
subtitle_i18n.hi: कैसे एक बंबई व्यापारी ने साम्राज्य को तौला और उसे कमतर पाया
